items.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009
items.q: a drummer, Brad Hunter, anyway, he worked with the Federal Jazz Commission once or twice, and I asked him

ctx.x: I don’t know why. I understand what you’re saying and yes it’s absolutely true. I mean some of the music that becomes popular and stays popular attracts a larger audience and more money as well. I mean stadiums full of people for Springsteen and things like that. As I said, Carnegie Hall wasn’t full when we played there. But I have no idea. A lot of people say it sounds so much the same. Whatever tune you play, whether it’s fast or slow,

even a specific melody, it still sounds the same. Well it’s got a structure to it. You know? And if you stay pretty much within that structure it’s going to sound a little bit alike. The interplay between the horns and the rhythm section that’s playing behind them, and sometimes the tune itself will be without any solos, it’ll be all ensemble, with the horns in three part harmony or sometimes unison, but I just don’t know. I think that’s what somebody said to me. Now Dave Robinson has had this youth group. It…
I feel like Dixieland is very happy music most of the time?
